Most of all when a woman comes toward him: at once his look changes, his lips are like a boiling pot, his cheeks burn like coals of fire, his eyes flash like torches of lightning, and the lines of his face go astray, jumbled and distorted. So na'af carries a nun, the letter that marks being acted upon, because the look of the face is acted upon and changed. Na'af then means not the act of harlotry but the look of the face drawn from the urge to it, and the act took its name from the passing look that comes of it, just as anger itself is called af for the change it works on the face.

more.h: Why af serves only anger and lust
more.t: That is why af was borrowed only for anger and for adultery. Every other trait, pride and humility, jealousy and hatred, flattery and the like, also marks the face and testifies to its owner, yet a man can hide it and give himself a face as though he were the opposite of what he is. Not anger and lust: when the urge for either overpowers him, no stratagem helps him deny the stirring of his heart and keep his face as it was. It changes against his will, through the suddenness and force of the boiling blood that rises over all its banks and breaks out onto the face in a fierce flood.

more.h: Ni'uf only with a married woman
more.t: Chazal say there is ni'uf only with a married woman, and Rav Pappenheim holds that this is because ni'uf speaks of the changed face of the adulterer. With a married woman the face changes far more than in other harlotry, since the adulterer bears two fears, fear of shame lest people notice him and fear of punishment from the husband if he notices; lust grows in the measure of the fear, there being no pleasure like completing a deed bound up with many dangers. So the face of one with a married woman, compounded of fear and dread with longing and lust, cannot but change into many colours, and ni'uf is said above all of a married woman.

Na'af in the light form differs from mena'ef in the heavy, and no'efes from mena'efes. The light: מות יומת הנואף והנואפת, "the adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death" (Vayikra 20:10). The heavy: זרע מנאף ותזנה, "seed of an adulterer, and she played the harlot" (Yeshayahu 57:3); כן דרך אשה מנאפת, "so is the way of an adulterous woman" (Mishlei 30:20). The light form is what he undergoes from the woman; the heavy is the things he does so that the woman is moved by him to desire, such as winking with his eyes. So a woman moved by the man is called no'efes, in the light form, and one who uses deeds and gestures to rouse the man's longing is mena'efes, in the heavy.

ער.sense: Bare: what lies open to the eye with nothing screening it. From it nakedness, skin and blindness, city and forest, the heap, waking and youth, the foe, and cunning.

more.t: A thing open to sight with nothing screening it is ער. Taking a cover off a thing is גלוי, uncovering, whose opposite is כסוי, covering, the putting on of a cover (he refers to the root גל). Taking off a thing's peel is חשף: what the language of the Talmud calls קליפה, peeling, the holy tongue calls חשף, as חשף חשפה והשליך (Yoel 1:7), he has stripped it bare and cast it away, and the verb ויחשף יערות (Tehillim 29:9), and strips the forests bare. But a thing that is exposed of itself, not hidden from the eye and with nothing on it to cover it, is ער.

דק מחספס (Shemos 16:14), a fine thing, husk-like or peeled: either it had a husk like the husk of millet and rice, or it was like a thing whose husk had been taken off. מחשף הלבן (Bereishis 30:37), laying bare the white: peeling white strips from the white bark on the rods. From peeling the word was borrowed for other kinds of uncovering: וחשופי שת (Yeshayahu 20:4), with buttocks bared, and ולחשף מים מגבא (Yeshayahu 30:14), to skim water from a cistern, which is taking off the top surface of the water, itself like a peel.

more.h: עריה and עירם, bare and naked
more.t: The noun for the condition is עריה, bareness: עריה תעור קשתך (Chavakuk 3:9), Your bow is laid bare, the bow uncovered and left bare. In ואת ערם ועריה (Yechezkel 16:7), and you were naked and bare, ערם is being without clothing, and עריה is lacking anything else to screen the body. He comes back to it later: עירם is said of the lack of clothing, and עריה of the lack of the body's other needs.

The verbs: את-שארו הערה (Vayikra 20:19), he has laid bare his own flesh, that is, uncovered; כי ארזה ערה (Tzefaniah 2:14), for He has laid bare its cedar work, in the sense of ויחשף יערות, and strips the forests bare, and חשף חשפה, he has stripped it bare; and so פשטה וערה (Yeshayahu 32:11), strip and make yourselves bare, and אשר הערה למות נפשו (Yeshayahu 53:12), because he laid bare his soul to death.

ערות על-יאור (Yeshayahu 19:7), the shoots by the Nile: plants at the start of their showing are called ערות, a word of uncovering, since no earth covers them any longer. So ומתערה כאזרח רענן (Tehillim 37:35), showing himself like a fresh native tree: he appears at the very start of his growing like a fresh native tree. Or ומתערה is from shaking out, shaking himself out and spreading like a fresh tree; and the sense is one, since shaking out too belongs to ער and uncovering.

more.h: Shaking out, with and without nun
more.t: What shakes itself out is left bare of what was in it, and what is shaken out of a vessel is left bare, with the vessel no longer covering it: ותער כדה אל-השקת (Bereishis 24:20), she emptied her jar into the trough, where pouring out the water left the jar bare; and תשכרי ותתערי (Eichah 4:21), you shall be drunk and lay yourself bare. The word is found with a nun, וינער (Shemos 14:27), Hashem shook out Mitzrayim, and התנערי מעפר קומי (Yeshayahu 52:2), shake yourself from the dust, arise; and without it, ותער כדה, she emptied her jar, and אל תער נפשי (Tehillim 141:8), do not pour out my soul. The waste shaken out of flax is נעורת, tow: כאשר ינתק פתיל-הנערת (Shoftim 16:9), as a strand of tow snaps, and והיה החסן לנערת (Yeshayahu 1:31), and the strong shall become tow.

From shaking out is מערה, a cave, as וישב במערה, and he dwelt in a cave, and מערת המכפלה, the cave of Machpelah: it is so called because it is emptied out of the ground. The verb is ערו ערו עד היסוד בה (Tehillim 137:7), lay it bare, lay it bare, to its foundation; and he sets beside it כמער-איש וליות (Melachim I 7:36), by the clear space of each, with wreaths.

From uncovering is ערוה, uncovering in a bad sense: a thing whose exposure is unseemly. לראות את-ערות הארץ (Bereishis 42:9), to see the nakedness of the land; לכסות בשר ערוה (Shemos 28:42), to cover the flesh of nakedness; ערות אביך וערות אמך (Vayikra 18:7), the nakedness of your father and the nakedness of your mother; and כי מצא בה ערות דבר (Devarim 24:1), for he has found in her an unseemly matter, which is conduct with licentiousness and exposure, the opposite of modesty.

One lacking children or any other family tie is ערירי: ואנכי הולך ערירי (Bereishis 15:2), and I go childless, without children and without any support from family. It is an adjective from ער and uncovering: children and family are to a man like clothing and a cover to the body, and without them he stands like a naked body with no shelter.

From the same sense is ערער, a tree whose leaves have fallen and whose branches have dried, standing bare: והיה כערער בערבה (Yirmiyahu 17:6), he shall be like a bare tree in the desert, and כערוער במדבר (Yirmiyahu 48:6), like a bare tree in the wilderness. So פנה אל תפלת הערער (Tehillim 102:18), He turned to the prayer of the bare one, the prayer of one like the ערער tree, cast off and forsaken by all; and the verb, ערער תתערער (Yirmiyahu 51:58), shall be utterly laid bare. It may be, Rav Pappenheim adds, that ערירי and ערער are from shaking out: one emptied and void of everything, whether of family or of natural plenty.

From uncovering is עור, skin: כתנות עור (Bereishis 3:21), garments of skin; עורות גדיי העזים (Bereishis 27:16), the skins of the young goats; ועורות תחשים (Shemos 25:5), and tachash skins; הוא שמלתו לעורו (Shemos 22:26), it is his garment for his skin. It is called עור from uncovering, since it alone stands bare and all the other parts of the body are covered by it.

more.h: עור, blind: a skin over the eye
more.t: From עור, skin, comes עור, blind, and עורון, blindness: או פקח או עור (Shemos 4:11), or seeing or blind; כי השחד יעור (Shemos 23:8), for the bribe blinds. Blindness is a skin rising over the eye: a film that forms from some fluid, congeals, spreads over the eye and blocks sight. This kind of blindness is commoner than the blindness that comes of the eye being put out or of the fluid in it drying up, and so every lack of sight is called עורון, after the skin-film, the commonest and most usual kind.

ואת עיני צדקיהו עור (Yirmiyahu 39:7), and he blinded the eyes of Tzidkiyahu: since it does not say that he put out his eyes, as is written of Shimshon, וינקרו את עיניו (Shoftim 16:21), and they put out his eyes, and as in העיני האנשים ההם תנקר? (Bamidbar 16:14), will you put out the eyes of those men?, it seems that he did not put out Tzidkiyahu's eyes but smeared them with some drug that blinds, as though a skin were spread over them. So כי השחד יעור (Shemos 23:8) does not mean that the bribe ruins the eyes of the mind for good, so that they cannot see even at another time when there is no bribe. It means that while he takes a bribe he is blind, the bribe rising like a film over his eyes and covering the sight of the truth; at another time, with no bribe and no film to cover them, he sees well again.

From uncovering is עיר, a city: נבנה לנו עיר (Bereishis 11:4), let us build ourselves a city; עיר חומה (Vayikra 25:29), a walled city; וערי מבצר (Yehoshua 19:35), and the fortified cities: for a city has streets and markets that stand open to everyone. The opposite of a city is כפר, a village: נלינה בכפרים (Shir HaShirim 7:12), let us lodge in the villages, a word of covering, in the sense of וכפרת אותה (Bereishis 6:14), and you shall cover it. A village has no exposed open spaces; it is like a courtyard, and so it is also called חצר: ובתי החצרים (Vayikra 25:31), and the houses of the villages, and בחצריהם ובטירותם (Bereishis 25:16), by their villages and by their encampments.

יער, a forest: יבא את רעהו ביער (Devarim 19:5), he goes into the forest with his fellow; חיתו יער (Tehillim 50:10), the beasts of the forest; כתפוח בעצי היער (Shir HaShirim 2:3), like an apple tree among the trees of the forest; יער צומח עצים (Koheles 2:6), a forest sprouting trees. Any tract of trees gathered together that bear no fruit is יער, from uncovering: since its trees carry no fruit, it stands exposed, not ringed by a fence. Its opposite is גן, a garden, from protecting and covering: a tract of fruit trees and vegetables, ringed by a fence to guard it against loss (he refers to the root גן).

Honey too is called יער, after its place. Most bees' honey is found in forests, since the bees gather the honey and the wax from the blossoms of the forest's trees, and even where no hives are made for them they make hives for themselves in the forest trees. So ביערת הדבש (Shmuel I 14:27), in the comb of honey, and אכלתי יערי עם דבשי (Shir HaShirim 5:1), I have eaten my forest honey with my honey: יערי is the forest's honey, which comes from the bees, and דבשי is the honey that comes from dates.

תער, a razor: והעבירו תער על כל בשרם (Bamidbar 8:7), and let them pass a razor over all their flesh; כתער מלטש (Tehillim 52:4), like a sharpened razor. It is from uncovering, since it leaves the skin of the flesh bare of hair. The opposite is כסום יכסמו את ראשיהם (Yechezkel 44:20), they shall keep their heads trimmed, a word of covering (he refers to the root כס).

more.h: תער, a sheath, from shaking out
more.t: A sword's sheath is also called תער: וישלפה מתערה (Shmuel I 17:51), and he drew it from its sheath; תצא חרבי מתערה (Yechezkel 21:9), My sword shall go out of its sheath. This תער is not from uncovering, as the shaving razor is, but from shaking out: the sword shakes itself out of the sheath, which is left emptied and void of it, and so the sheath itself is called תער. It is in the sense of אריק חרבי (Shemos 15:9), I will draw my sword, meaning I will empty the sheath of the sword, and שמן תורק שמך (Shir HaShirim 1:3), your name is oil poured out, named for the vessel that is emptied. So too the German calls a sword's sheath שיידע, Scheide, a word of separating, since the sword separates from it.

more.h: ערום, naked, with an added mem
more.t: From ער, uncovering, with a mem added, comes the adjective ערום, lacking clothing, so that one's flesh is exposed: ויהיו שניהם ערומים (Bereishis 2:25), and the two of them were naked; כי-עירם אנכי (Bereishis 3:10), for I am naked; the adjective for the masculine, and in the feminine פן-אפשיטנה ערמה (Hoshea 2:5), lest I strip her naked. Sometimes עירם is the noun for the condition: ואת ערם ועריה (Yechezkel 16:7), and you were naked and bare, and בהיותך עירם ועריה (Yechezkel 16:22), when you were naked and bare, that is, one possessed of nakedness, found in the state of nakedness.

From ערום, the lack of clothing, comes ערמה, a heap: ויבא לשכב בקצה הערמה (Rus 3:7), and he came to lie down at the end of the heap; בטנך ערמת חטים (Shir HaShirim 7:3), your belly is a heap of wheat. A pile of threshed grain is called ערמה because the grain has been stripped of the straw that was its clothing and has become naked; and the stack made of it is called ערמה because it is gathered from naked grain. The opposite is the גדיש, which is gathered from grain still in its ears.

By borrowing, וברוח אפיך נערמו מים (Shemos 15:8), and with the breath of Your nostrils the waters were heaped up: they became waves upon waves, like heaps of grain. Or it is from ערום in its plain sense: the upper waters at the surface cover the lower ones, and when the wind blew the upper waters swelled up and the lower were left naked.
A kind of tree is called ערמון (Bereishis 30:37) because it has no branches below, only above at its top, and so stands naked and stripped of branches, like a naked man without clothing.

Also from uncovering is the verb ער, rousing, waking and motion: כנשר יעיר קנו (Devarim 32:11), as an eagle stirs up its nest; עוררה את גבורתך (Tehillim 80:3), rouse Your might; עורה למה תישן (Tehillim 44:24), awake, why do You sleep?; והוא עורר את-חניתו (Shmuel II 23:18), and he roused his spear; שנאה תערר מדנים (Mishlei 10:12), hatred stirs up strife; מה תעירו ומה תעררו (Shir HaShirim 8:4), why would you wake, why would you rouse: that they not wake her from her sleep, nor rouse her to show herself. Whatever shows itself in motion and in deed, as against lying hidden and concealed within itself, is called ער.

more.h: נער, youth, the time of rousing
more.t: From this is נער, with נערות and נעורים, youth: the time of youth, when a person is still in rousing, motion and wakefulness, as against old age, when the body's powers weaken and a person is like one drowsy and weary. So the young man is called נער, a word of rousing, in the sense of נערו כגורי אריות (Yirmiyahu 51:38), they rouse themselves like lion cubs. והנער נער (Shmuel I 1:24), and the youth was a youth, means that he had extra liveliness; and כי היה נער ואדמני (Shmuel I 17:42), for he was a youth, and ruddy, means that he had extra rousing, a thing felt in a youth's movements. The female in her youth is called נערה, just as עלם and עלמה are from עליה, rising (he refers to the root על).

So too עיר, the young horse and donkey: ועירם עשרה (Bereishis 32:16), and ten foals; אסרי לגפן עירה (Bereishis 49:11), binding his foal to the vine; והאלפים והעירים (Yeshayahu 30:24), the oxen and the young donkeys; ועל עיר בן אתנות (Zecharyah 9:9), and upon a foal, the son of she-donkeys. It too is named for rousing, for the extra wakefulness in it.

ער is also an enemy: ויהי ערך (Shmuel I 28:16), and has become your enemy; נשוא לשוא עריך (Tehillim 139:20), Your enemies lift it up in vain. It is from rousing and rising up, like מתקוממים, those who rise up against one: one who hates another is roused against him whenever he sees him or remembers him (he refers to the root אב). Or ער is uncovering in its plain sense, an open enemy who no longer hides his hatred: there is an enemy who covers his hatred in his heart, and when his hatred grows until he shows it to the other, he is called ער.

From ער and rousing too is ערם, with ערמה, cunning, which is sharpness and wakefulness of mind. A man may have great intelligence and yet know how to use it only in its usual way, and not otherwise, by stratagem (as the matter sometimes demands, when it can be reached only by stratagem); for that he has no capacity, his mind being as though dozing and asleep, not looking about for any way to reach what he seeks. One who has the capacity and the knowledge to use his mind in different ways is called ערום, from the wakefulness and alertness of his mind, poised to spread to every side of the possible: והנחש היה ערום (Bereishis 3:1), and the serpent was cunning, since enticing the woman to do a thing whose penalty was death needed extra stratagem.

more.h: Cunning for good and for ill
more.t: Every work of the mind has a side for praise and a side for blame: wise to do good and wise to do evil, a man of מזימה, sound design, and a man of זימה, wicked design. So ערמה has a use for blame and a use for praise. For blame: להרגו בערמה (Shemos 21:14), to kill him by guile; מפר מחשבות ערומים (Iyov 5:12), He frustrates the designs of the crafty; על-עמך יערימו סוד (Tehillim 83:4), against Your people they lay crafty counsel. For praise: ויעשו גם-המה בערמה (Yehoshua 9:4), they too acted with cunning; לתת לפתאים ערמה (Mishlei 1:4), to give prudence to the simple; וערומים יכתרו דעת (Mishlei 14:18), and the prudent are crowned with knowledge; ערום ראה רעה ונסתר (Mishlei 22:3), the prudent man sees evil and hides.

The sense of ערמה is found without the mem as well: ער וענה מאהלי יעקב (Malachi 2:12), the one awake and the one who answers, from the tents of Yaakov, that is, diligent and sharp, whose mind is awake. It is like עצם, the shutting of the eyes, found with a mem, ועצם עיניו (Yeshayahu 33:15), and shuts his eyes, and also without it, עצה עיניו (Mishlei 16:30), he shuts his eyes, with one sense; so too ערם and ער.

בא.sense: Coming: joining the fixed goal one moves toward, the opposite of going out. From ב, the letter of attachment, it holds both the motion to a place and the arrival in it.

more.t: Coming is joining the boundary one is heading for, the opposite of going out (יציאה), which is parting from a boundary. It is a relative term, said only with respect to the boundary that is its end, and only where that boundary is fixed and stays in its place. Where it is not fixed, one cannot say of the one coming that his coming is complete: one may say that he drew near or approached (שקרב או נגש), but not that he came. Where it is fixed, בא is said even while he is still on the way, since he must reach it in the end: והנה עשו בא (Bereishis 33:1), and behold, Esav was coming, though he had not yet arrived; as he draws ever nearer to the fixed point, we see it as though the coming were already complete. And ביאה, coming, is said only of one who, having reached the boundary he sought, stops moving; of one who is still in motion it is not clear that the coming is complete.

more.h: The sun comes only when it sets
more.t: So בא is said of the sun only at its setting, כי בא השמש (Bereishis 28:11), for the sun had come in, and not at its rising. From where we stand it would fit the sunrise better, since we are the boundary and the sun comes toward us; but after rising it is still in motion and does not rest, so ביאה, coming, does not apply to it. When it sets and we no longer see it moving, we may say כי באה, for it has come, as though it had found the point it sought on the western horizon and come to rest there.

The noun of place is מבוא, an entry: מבוא השמש (Devarim 11:30), the going in of the sun, and מבוא העיר (Shoftim 1:24), the entry of the city. In the language of Chazal it is מבוי, as מבוי שהוא גבוה (Eruvin), an alley that is high, on the pattern of ראוי, fit, and מצוי, found; in the plural מבואות, as שתופי מבואות (Eruvin 79b), the partnerships of the alleys. A מבוי, then, is the entry of the street: not the street itself, though it takes in both; what is meant is the open space of the street through which one comes into the houses and courtyards.

more.h: To bring, and the verb's other forms
more.t: The verb of bringing is הביא, he brought, and מובא, brought: כי הובאו בית יוסף (Bereishis 43:18), that they had been brought into Yosef's house, that is, made to come by another. The verb is never found in the simple passive, so that it should not be confused with נביא, prophet, and נבואה, prophecy. It comes without its alef, ויבו ירבעם (Melachim I 12:12), and Yeravam came, and הנני מבי עליך (Melachim I 21:21), behold, I am bringing upon you; and with a tav added, תבואתה לראש יוסף (Devarim 33:16), let it come upon the head of Yosef, and תבואתך טובה (Iyov 22:21), good will come to you.

From the root comes תבואה, what the ground grows, grain and the fruit of trees alike: כתבואת גרן וכתבואת יקב (Bamidbar 18:30), as the yield of the threshing floor and as the yield of the winepress. It is named for the bringing forth that the earth brings. It is a noun of the verb, but not of the simple form, since it does not speak of coming; it is of the causative, which speaks of bringing. The sense is that of יבול, what the earth carries forth; see his explanation at the root בל. It is said also of the fruit of thought and deed: ותבואתי מכסף נבחר (Mishlei 8:19), and my yield is better than choice silver; תבואת רשע לחטאת (Mishlei 10:16), the yield of the wicked is for sin; תבואת שפתיו ישבע (Mishlei 18:20), with the yield of his lips he is sated.

more.h: Whoever loves a crowd has no yield
more.t: ומי אוהב בהמון לא תבואה (Koheles 5:9), and whoever loves a crowd has no yield: the one who loves a crowd of workers to do his work, for some people love bustle and like their affairs run on a large scale. Such a man never makes a profit and gains nothing from the many hands, for ברבות הטובה רבו אוכליה (Koheles 5:10), when good increases, those who eat it increase, and his wage goes out in his loss: as the good grows with the number of workers, so grows the need to feed and keep them. The householder has no advantage כי אם ראות עיניו, but the sight of his eyes: many people reclining at his table and his house in a tumult. Better to have few workers and to work alongside them himself, for מתוקה שנת העובד (Koheles 5:11), sweet is the sleep of the worker, who enjoys the toil of his hands, whether much or little. Not so the rich man who slackens in the work because he relies on his many workers: though his provisions are plentiful, his sleep is confused and troubled.

more.h: נביא, the one who brings words
more.t: From בא in the sense of bringing comes the noun נביא, prophet, on the pattern of נשיא, prince, and נזיר, nazirite. He is the messenger who brings the words of Hashem to the people and the words of the people to Hashem, and he is called נביא for this bringing of words, as it says והבאת אתה את הדברים אל האלהים (Shemos 18:19), and you shall bring the matters to Hashem. That is the chief condition of a prophet: that he stand so high that Hashem attends to him, makes him His messenger to tell the people His words, and receives the people's words through him. Working signs and wonders beyond nature, and knowing the future, are incidental to a prophet, for times when the hour requires them, and are not a necessary condition: many prophets prophesied of whom no miracles or foretelling became known. וידע כל ישראל כי נאמן שמואל לנביא (Shmuel I 3:20), and all Yisrael knew that Shmuel was established as a prophet, when he had not yet worked any wonder; they knew he was a prophet because Hashem had revealed Himself to him.

ואהרן אחיך יהיה נביאך (Shemos 7:1), and Aharon your brother shall be your prophet: the one who brings your words to Pharaoh, as a prophet brings the words of Hashem to the people, so that you are in My place and he in yours. And of the one who prophesied at the king's direction, הניבא על ידי המלך, it says הנבא על הודות והלל (Divrei HaYamim I 25:2-3), who prophesied in thanksgiving and praise: that is, who brought through songs the words of the king, and words of thanksgiving and praise to Hashem.

Telling the future is also called נבואה, prophecy, because it is found only among prophets and not among ordinary men. Hashem reveals His secret only to His servants the prophets (Amos 3:7), and works signs and wonders only through them, so that it should be clear to every challenger that they are His messengers, or to warn the people and set them straight in His ways.

more.h: נביא and רואה, prophet and seer
more.t: In time people made the secondary thing the main one, held that a prophet's chief distinction was to see what is to come, and called the prophet רואה, seer. This was in the days of the Judges, when over the years the principle the nation had received from of old was shaken: that the condition of a prophet is his mission and not foretelling. Thinking foretelling the main thing, they set aside the name נביא, which speaks of bringing the mission, and called him רואה, for the seeing of the future. So כי לנביא היום יקרא לפנים הרואה (Shmuel I 9:9), for the one now called a prophet was formerly called a seer. היום, today, refers to the time Shmuel wrote his book, at the end of his life, when the name רואה had fallen away again and נביא had been chosen again as at first. Writing then, Shmuel was saying: what I now call a prophet, by the true name it had in early days, was called before, in the days of the Judges and in the years of my youth as well, a seer.

more.h: The root is the letter ב
more.t: In the word בא the only root letter is ב, and the alef is added: it is missing in the forms above and in ויכל מהתנבות (Shmuel I 10:13), and he finished prophesying. The letter ב in itself marks the cleaving of a quality (מקרה) to the thing that bears it (נושא), that is, the boundary it is in: בי, בהם, בכם, in me, in them, in you. Since there are many ways for a quality to cleave to its bearer, ב has many uses.

Some qualities cleave from the start, as heat to fire and wetness to water, from their creation: יהיה בו מום (Vayikra 21:17), who has a blemish in him, and או תבלול בעינו (Vayikra 21:20), or a film in his eye. Some arise anew, as flowing in water that is sometimes still and sometimes running: כי יהיה בו שבר רגל (Vayikra 21:19), who has a broken leg, for the break is not from his creation. What arises may come about in place, as flowing within the water itself: כי פשה הנגע בבית (Vayikra 14:48), that the plague has spread in the house; ושער שחור צמח בו (Vayikra 13:37), and black hair has grown in it; ויהי רעב בארץ (Bereishis 12:10), and there was famine in the land. Or it may come upon the bearer from outside, as warmth comes upon water: כאשר יתן מום באדם כן ינתן בו (Vayikra 24:20), as he put a blemish in a man so shall it be put in him; ורחץ במים (Vayikra 14:8), and he shall wash in water; ודבק באשתו (Bereishis 2:24), and he shall cleave to his wife. What comes from outside sometimes comes through a means, as rinsing is done by means of water: ומורק ושטף במים (Vayikra 6:21), it shall be scoured and rinsed in water; מיד האמורי בחרבי ובקשתי (Bereishis 48:22), from the hand of the Emori with my sword and my bow; and this is what is called the ב of the instrument.

Some cleaving arises inside the bearer: והשוכב בבית (Vayikra 14:47), and one who lies in the house; בבית ובשדה (Bereishis 39:5), in the house and in the field; ובדרך לא היה (Bamidbar 9:13), and was not on the road. Some is by leaning on it: לא בקשתי אבטח (Tehillim 44:7), not in my bow do I trust; הנוגע בהר (Shemos 19:12), whoever touches the mountain. Some is by company: כי במקלי עברתי את הירדן (Bereishis 32:11), for with my staff I crossed the Yarden; בזאת יבא אהרן (Vayikra 16:3), with this shall Aharon come. Some is in time, either the time itself, בעת ההיא (Yehoshua 5:2), at that time, בימים ההם (Bereishis 6:4), in those days, ויכל אלהים ביום השביעי (Bereishis 2:2), and Hashem finished on the seventh day; or through some act in between, ובלכתך בדרך ובשכבך ובקומך (Devarim 6:7), and as you walk on the way, and as you lie down and as you rise, and ובמלאות ימי טהרה (Vayikra 12:6), and when the days of her purity are complete. The act in between may mark the time by chance, as בשכון ישראל (Bereishis 35:22), when Yisrael dwelt, וברדת הטל (Bamidbar 11:9), and when the dew came down, and בשבתך בביתך (Devarim 6:7), when you sit in your house; or be bound to the time necessarily, as ובשכבך ובקומך (Devarim 6:7), at the hour people lie down; בעלותך לראות (Shemos 34:24), when you go up to appear; באכלכם מלחם הארץ (Bamidbar 15:19), when you eat of the bread of the land; באין אלפים אבוס בר (Mishlei 14:4), where there are no oxen the trough is clean, that is, at a time when there are none; and התשחית בחמשה (Bereishis 18:28), will You destroy for the five, that is, at a time when five are lacking.

Some cleaving is a joining of things in imagination and thought: בכסף מלא יתננה לי (Bereishis 23:9), for full silver let him give it to me, an imagined joining of the act of giving to the receipt of full silver; והנותר בבשר ובלחם (Vayikra 8:32), and what is left of the flesh and of the bread, where being left over is attached to the flesh and bread by a relation in thought. So too ותדבר מרים ואהרן במשה (Bamidbar 12:1), and Miriam and Aharon spoke against Moshe; ויעבד ישראל באשה (Hoshea 12:13), and Yisrael served for a wife; כפלים בכל חטאותיה (Yeshayahu 40:2), double for all her sins; בך ארוץ גדוד (Shmuel II 22:30), by You I run against a troop; לדבקה בו (Devarim 11:22), to cleave to Him. All these, and many more, are the cleaving of a quality to its bearer: from the start or arising anew, from within the bearer itself or by coming from outside.

more.h: Two stages, ל and ב, make בא
more.t: A quality that comes from outside must pass two stages. First the motion, in which it moves to cleave to its bearer: the preparation and the act before the attachment. Then the attachment itself, the point of time at which it takes hold and is complete, the outcome of the motion before it. The letter ל marks the motion that comes before, which the logicians call מאמר לו, the category of to it, motion toward some point, matter or state; the letter ב marks the attachment once complete, which they call מאמר בו, the category of in it. German says both with its word for in: of one walking in the city, געהט אין דער שטאט, geht in der Stadt, he walks in the city, and of one going to the city, געהט אין דיא שטאט, geht in die Stadt, he goes into the city; it tells the two apart by the article, die or der, the word der, which Rav Pappenheim labels genitive, meaning the inside of the city. So ב serves for the cleaving of a quality to its bearer, from within or from outside, and from its use for what comes from outside the language made the word בא, to come: the verb that gathers both stages. Before the joining is complete the one coming is in motion toward the boundary he heads for, in the category of to it; once he has cleaved to that boundary he passes out of the category of to it into the category of in it, and the verb that holds both is called בא.

גז.sense: Shearing: a cut that takes off the upper or outer part while the main body remains; unlike shaving, which is of hair alone and cuts close to the skin.

more.t: גלוח, shaving, is said specifically of hair, whether of the beard, the head or the rest of the body, and it is razor-like, cutting the hair close to the flesh. It may be for grooming and adornment, as ויגלח ויחלף שמלתיו (Bereishis 41:14), and he shaved and changed his garments, or for disfigurement and spoiling, as וגלחה את ראשה (Devarim 21:12), and she shall shave her head. גזיזה, shearing, is said of anything cut so that some of it remains: of hair, as ויגז את ראשו (Iyov 1:20), and he sheared his head; and of cutting the wool from the sheep, as גזזי צאנו (Bereishis 38:12), the shearers of his sheep, and לגז צאנו (Bereishis 38:13), to shear his sheep.
Cutting stones and dressing them is גזיזה as well: אבני גזית (Melachim I 5:31), hewn stones, are stones that were cut, straightened and cleared of the spurs that stuck out of them.

more.h: You are the One Who trims me
more.t: This is the sense of ממעי אמי אתה גוזי (Tehillim 71:6), from my mother's womb You are my trimmer, on the pattern of עושי and קוני, my Maker and my Possessor. That is: from the time I came out of my mother's womb until now You have always been the One Who trims me and sets me right, as a guardian does with an infant he rears, straightening it and setting it right all the time and taking from it whatever is waste or unsightly, in the manner of הוא עשך ויכננך (Devarim 32:6), He made you and established you. גוזי is a participle of the light form.
As a verb it sometimes comes with the zayin doubled, לגזז את צאנו (Bereishis 31:19), to shear his sheep, and sometimes plain, לגז צאנו (Bereishis 38:13), to shear his sheep.

more.h: Quails cut off from the sea
more.t: ויגז שלוים מן הים (Bamidbar 11:31), and it cut off quails from the sea, is a quantity of quails cut off from the vast mass of them found on the seashore; for the quail is one of the birds that travel to the warm lands in the winter, and they always gather together on the shore of the sea.

In כי גז חיש ונעפה (Tehillim 90:10), for the cutting off comes swiftly and we fly away, גז is either an intransitive verb, on the pattern of קם and שב, rose and returned, or a transitive one, on the pattern of שת in כי שת לי אלהים זרע אחר (Bereishis 4:25), for Elokim has appointed me another offspring.
The noun of the verb is גז, in וראשית גז צאנך (Devarim 18:4), and the first of the fleece of your flock; with the feminine he it is גזה, in על הגזה לבדה (Shoftim 6:37), on the fleece alone.

גז is also a noun in ירד כמטר על גז (Tehillim 72:6), let him come down like rain upon the mown grass, and there it is not the גז of גז צאנך (Devarim 18:4), the fleece of your flock. The גז of the flock is what is shorn off; the גז in Tehillim is the grass that remains after the cutting.

A kind of locust is called גזם: יתר הגזם אכל הארבה (Yoel 1:4), what the gazam left the arbeh ate, and והחסיל והגזם (Yoel 2:25), and the chasil and the gazam. The mem is added, as in סלעם (Vayikra 11:22), a kind of locust found on the rocks, the סלעים; so גזם is from גז, named for the way it eats, shearing the greens.

Its companion, in וילק ואין מספר (Tehillim 105:34), and yelek without number, is named from מליקה, nipping, since it nips the greens; or from the sense of ילקו הכלבים (Melachim I 21:19), the dogs shall lick, which is to be explained under the root לק.

שב.sense: Return, to a former place or state or to the state nature calls for; and since rest is the natural state, ceasing from motion: sitting, captivity, Shabbos

more.t: The root's basic sense is return, a going back to what came before, and it comes in three kinds. The first is back to a former place: ויצא יצוא ושוב (Bereishis 8:7), it went out, going and returning; ותשב אליו אל התבה (Bereishis 8:9), she came back to him, to the ark; ודור רביעי ישובו הנה (Bereishis 15:16), the fourth generation shall return here. The second is back to a former condition: עד אשר תשוב חמת אחיך (Bereishis 27:44), until your brother's fury turns back; שוב מחרון אפך (Shemos 32:12), turn back from Your burning anger, that is, to the goodwill there was before; והנה שבה כבשרו (Shemos 4:7), and it had gone back to being like his flesh. Both have three stations and two moves: the thing leaves its first station for a second, then leaves that and goes back to the first.

The third kind has two stations and one move: a thing enters the state it ought to be in, by nature or by right, though it was never there before. One born blind who is healed is said to have שב לראיתו, returned to his sight, though he never saw; since nature calls for sight, it counts as his earlier station, and blindness as a removal from it. So ההשב אשיב את בנך אל הארץ אשר יצאת משם (Bereishis 24:5), shall I bring your son back to the land you came out of?, though Yitzchak had never been there: it was the land of his fathers' birth. So too תשובו לתוכחתי (Mishlei 1:23), turn back to my rebuke, since heeding rebuke is what the soul's nature calls for; and גם אל פיהו לא ישיבנה (Mishlei 19:24), he will not even bring it back to his mouth, since the hand meeting the mouth to eat is a natural need, and so השבה, bringing back, is said of it.

ובשוב צדיק מצדקתו ועשה עול (Yechezkel 18:24), when a righteous man turns from his righteousness and does wrong, does not by its plain sense speak of one who was wicked, became righteous and then went back to his wickedness, but of one who was always righteous and became wicked. Nor is ובשוב רשע מרשעתו (Yechezkel 18:27), when a wicked man turns from his wickedness, about one who was righteous, became wicked and turned righteous again because תוהא על הראשונות, he regrets the earlier ones, the reading Chazal give by way of derash (Kiddushin 40b). Rav Pappenheim's account is that man is set in two natures that oppose each other: his good inclination binds him to be good and his evil inclination binds him to be evil. A lifelong tzaddik who turns wicked has returned to the nature that binds him to evil, and a lifelong rasha who turns righteous has returned to the nature that binds him to righteousness, so תשובה, return, is said of both.

There is also a return of words: וישב משה את דברי העם (Shemos 19:8), Moshe brought back the people's words; וישיבו אותם דבר (Bamidbar 13:26), they brought back word to them; משיב דברים נכוחים (Mishlei 24:26), one who gives back straight words. Speech is like a messenger sent to bring something back, and the other man's answer is like the messenger coming back to the one who sent him, so תשובה, return, fits an answer.
With the bet doubled comes the noun שביב: ולא-יגה שביב אשו (Iyov 18:5), the spark of his fire will not shine. It is the spark of light that comes back when it falls on a hard body.

The verb שבב: וילך שובב בדרך לבו (Yeshayahu 57:17), he went on wayward in the way of his heart; שובו בנים שובבים (Yirmiyahu 3:14), return, wayward children. It is error and wandering: one who strives to reach a true goal and does not find it, since nothing he finds is the true one, and he must keep turning back and taking another road. So שובב is from תשובה, return, for he must always go back from the road he set out on. A deranged mind that cannot settle is also שובב: ושובבתיך ונתתי חחים (Yechezkel 38:4), I will turn you about and put hooks in you; משובבת מחרב (Yechezkel 38:8), turned about from the sword; ושבבתיך וששאתיך (Yechezkel 39:2), I will turn you about and lead you on.

So the twisting, confused road, where no way out can be found and one must go back to where one came from, is also שבב: רעיהם התעום הרים שובבום (Yirmiyahu 50:6), their shepherds led them astray, on mountains that turned them about, mountains so tangled that no way out of them is found, going always from mountain to hill and from hill to mountain; and כי שבבים יהיה עגל שמרון (Hoshea 8:6), for the calf of Shomron shall become shevavim, meaning the roads that lead to the calf of Shomron will be confused, and the road that brings one there will not be found.

The noun משבה belongs with these: משבה ישראל (Yirmiyahu 3:6), wayward Israel; ארפה משובתיכם (Yirmiyahu 3:22), I will heal your waywardness; משבה נצחת (Yirmiyahu 8:5), a lasting waywardness; ארפא משובתם (Hoshea 14:5), I will heal their waywardness.

more.h: Rest as a return to nature
more.t: From the first sense, return to what came earlier in time or to the natural state that comes first in rank, other nouns and verbs derive that all share one meaning, ceasing from motion, that is, rest, which is in truth a return to the natural state. Rest is a thing's natural state: a body is by nature at rest of itself, and rest involves no action and needs no cause to come about, while nothing moves without a cause, from outside or within, to move it. So a thing that stops moving is said to have שב, returned, to its natural state, which is rest.

That is the verb ישב, sitting, the end of moving about and the return to rest. Sometimes it is the body not moving, the opposite of walking and standing: יושב פתח האוהל (Bereishis 18:1), sitting at the entrance of the tent; קום נא שבה (Bereishis 27:19), rise, please, sit; וכל כלי אשר תשב עליו (Vayikra 15:20), and any vessel she sits on; היושב על כסאו (Shemos 11:5), who sits on his throne.

Sometimes it is no longer moving from place to place, and then it means staying: לשבת אברם בארץ כנען (Bereishis 16:3), of Avram's dwelling in the land of Canaan; בכל מושבותיכם (Shemos 12:20), in all your dwellings; ואשב בהר (Devarim 9:9), I stayed on the mountain; בסוכות תשבו (Vayikra 23:42), you shall dwell in sukkos; גר ותושב (Bereishis 23:4), a sojourner and a resident. One who stays in a land and fixes his dwelling there is called תושב, resident. So תשב על דמי טהרה (Vayikra 12:5), she shall remain in the blood of purity, means she shall stay.

From the end of moving about comes בשובה ונחת תושעון (Yeshayahu 30:15), in stillness and quiet you shall be saved, that is, מתון מתון (Berachos 20a), slowly, slowly, without much moving about. From this sense too is שובנו אלהי ישענו (Tehillim 85:5), settle us, Elokim of our salvation; and with the bet doubled, נפשי ישובב (Tehillim 23:3), He settles my soul, and לשובב יעקב אליו (Yeshayahu 49:5), to settle Yaakov with Him. Or it is from תשובה, return: לשובב is like להשיב, to bring back, as לרומם is like להרים, to raise, in לרומם את בית אלהינו (Ezra 9:9), to raise up the house of our Elokim.

With a nun, one of the formative letters, comes a verb נשב, from ישיבה, settling: וישב אתם אברם (Bereishis 15:11), and Avram blew them away; כי רוח יהוה נשבה בו (Yeshayahu 40:7), for the breath of Hashem blew upon it; ישב רוחו יזלו מים (Tehillim 147:18), He makes His wind blow and the waters flow. It is from settling: the wind that moves about enters and settles in the body that receives it.

Also from the stopping of motion is the verb שבה, captivity, which stops free natural movement: כי נשבה אחיו (Bereishis 14:14), that his brother had been taken captive; כשבויות חרב (Bereishis 31:26), like captives of the sword; וישב ממנו שבי (Bamidbar 21:1), he took captives from him; שבות יעקב (Yechezkel 39:25), the captivity of Yaakov; שבות בני עמון (Yirmiyahu 49:6), the captivity of the children of Ammon. Any stopping and cessation of moving by choice and will is called שביה, captivity.

For stopping occupation and the motion of work a tav is added: שבת, ceasing, an end to activity: שבת וינפש (Shemos 31:17), He ceased and rested; ושבתה הארץ (Vayikra 25:2), the land shall rest; תשביתו שאור מבתיכם (Shemos 12:15), you shall clear leaven out of your houses, meaning an end to dealing with leaven; שבת שבתון (Shemos 31:15), a Shabbos of complete rest; שחקו על משבתיה (Eichah 1:7), they mocked at her ceasing.

For stopping plain natural motion there is the verb שאב, drawing water: יוצאות לשאוב מים (Bereishis 24:13), coming out to draw water; עד שואב מימיך (Devarim 29:10), to the one who draws your water; ושאבתם מים בששון (Yeshayahu 12:3), you shall draw water in joy. Water brought into a vessel is stopped from flowing and moving with its natural motion. So the three are set apart by the motion each stops: שביה the movement of choice and will, שבת occupation and work, שאב the plain motion of nature; and Rav Pappenheim calls שאב close to שביה, in which the captive is stopped from the movement of his own choice.

עם.sense: With: the incidental sharing one relation with the essential, or the secondary with the main; at root ע, movement, so existence at one and the same time.

more.t: He classes עם as a particle (מלה). It is the relation shared between an accident and a substance, or between a main thing and a secondary one, and it is said of the incidental party, in that it is present in the same relation the essential party is in: ויהי שם עם יהוה (Shemos 34:28), and he was there with Hashem; עם המלך (Shmuel I 20:5), with the king; באה עם הצאן (Bereishis 29:6), coming with the sheep. With suffixes: עמי, with me; עמו, with him; עמך, with you; עמם, with them, as in הולך עמם לשלחם (Bereishis 18:16), going with them to send them off; or עמהם, as in לא תלך עמהם (Bamidbar 22:12), you shall not go with them.

Leaving the shared relation takes the mem of removal: ויצא מעמך (Vayikra 25:41), he shall go out from with you; מעמו (Shmuel I 18:13), from with him; מעמהם, from with them. With the ayin concealed: והסיר יהוה ממך (Devarim 7:15), and Hashem will remove from you; and ממכם, from you all: ממך and ממכם are מעמך and מעמכם, from with you.

At times עם stands as if it were the object itself, as in כחסד אשר עשיתי עמך (Bereishis 21:23), according to the kindness I did with you. That is not the sense of האיש אשר עשיתי עמו (Rus 2:19), the man with whom I worked, where both were working, he and she. Here only Avimelech acted, and Avraham received the act; yet עם is still the right word, since the kindness is an incidental act that attaches itself to Avraham's very self. So too אם תעשה עמנו רעה (Bereishis 26:29), that you do us no harm, and אשר אני עושה עמך (Shemos 34:10), which I am doing with you.
How עם differs from the particle את Rav Pappenheim sets out under the root את, not here.

more.h: The verb עמם, joined in relation
more.t: From the particle the framer of the language made a verb, עמם, for the joining of accident with substance, just as ותהינו לעלות ההרה (Devarim 1:41), you made ready to go up the mountain, is made from הן, behold. ארזים לא-עממהו (Yechezkel 31:8), the cedars were not with it: they did not enter with it into one relation, which is to say לא דמו אליו, they were not like it. Likewise כל סתום לא עממוך (Yechezkel 28:3), no hidden thing stood with you, meaning there was nothing hidden. And איכה יועם זהב (Eichah 4:1), how the gold is mixed: fine gold must have nothing foreign with it and be clean of all waste and dross, so יועם names the opposite, gold mixed in with other things.

Adding the nun of the passive form makes the noun נעם from עם, meaning pleasantness: ואת הארץ כי נעמה (Bereishis 49:15), and the land, that it was pleasant; מה יפית ומה נעמת (Shir HaShirim 7:7), how fair you are and how pleasant.

As Rav Pappenheim says he has shown many times in this work, no physical good or bad is something essential in the thing that bears it; each is a relation that comes about with the receiving sense, as it agrees with that sense or opposes it. What agrees with the receiving sense is called טוב, good, and what opposes it רע, bad. So עריבות, sweetness, comes from התערבות, mixing in with the sense; טעם, taste, from נטיעה, planting (see the root טע); and נעם, pleasantness, from עמיות, being with: a good agreement and attachment with the sense. The German speaker likewise says of a thing well received "es geht mit", it goes with.

The abstract noun from עם is עמת: the side that stands in one relation with the side over against it, when the two are on two sides, as לעמת המסגרת (Shemos 25:27), alongside the frame; or with the side next to it, when they are on one side, as לעמת העצה יסירנה (Vayikra 3:9), he shall remove it alongside the backbone. It is said of sharing in number, as לעמת קלעי החצר (Shemos 38:18), corresponding to the hangings of the courtyard; of order, one thing related to the next, as משמר, a watch, and לעמת משמר (Divrei HaYamim I 26:16), alongside a watch; and of quality, where one has what the other has or its opposite, as כל-עמת שבא כן ילך (Koheles 5:15), just as he came so shall he go, and גם את-זה לעמת-זה (Koheles 7:14), this one too alongside that one. Every עמת is from עם, sharing with a thing in some relation or other, and he takes עמת to mean עמיות, being with, as זולת, besides, comes from זל (see the root זל).
The difference between עמת, alongside; מול, in front of; נכח, facing; לקראת, toward; and נגד, opposite, he sets out at length in his Yerios Shlomo, under נגד, and not here.

As the noun עמת comes from עם, so does the adjective עמית: ואל אשת עמיתך (Vayikra 18:20), and to your fellow's wife; או קנה מיד עמיתך (Vayikra 25:14), or buy from your fellow's hand; ועל גבר עמיתי (Zecharyah 13:7), and against the man who is My fellow. From עם, with, it is the one who stands with you in a relation of brotherhood and friendship, or in some other civic or religious relation. Rav Pappenheim allows too that עמית may come from עם with a patach, a people, and then means in particular one's fellow who is of his own people.

From עם, with, comes עם with a patach: a body of persons who share with one another some relation of quality or of character. הן עם אחד (Bereishis 11:6), they are one people; כל העם מקצה (Bereishis 19:4), all the people from every quarter; וישתחו לעם הארץ (Bereishis 23:7), and he bowed to the people of the land, where those alike in the traits of the common crowd are called together עם הארץ, the people of the land. הנמלים עם לא עז (Mishlei 30:25), the ants are a people not strong, sharing one particular quality.

Every large body holds smaller bodies alike in a quality that does not extend over the whole kind. The men of Europe share one quality that sets them apart from the men of Africa, and so are called עם אייראפא, the people of Europe; it divides again into many peoples, the French, the Germans and the like, each set apart from the next in some way and each called a people of its own; and each people divides again into lands, families and fathers' houses, each set apart in some quality, as one might say the men of such a land are warriors and the men of such a family given to anger and strife. Each is called עם for its sharing in one particular matter.

Since within every people are many smaller peoples, עם comes mostly in the plural, said of the great body: ויאסף אל עמיו (Bereishis 25:8), and he was gathered to his peoples; ונכרת מעמיו (Shemos 30:33), and he shall be cut off from his peoples; ונכרתה מעמיה (Vayikra 23:29), it shall be cut off from its peoples; לא יטמא בעל בעמיו (Vayikra 21:4), a husband shall not make himself impure among his peoples; אחריך בנימין בעממיך (Shoftim 5:14), after you, Binyamin, among your peoples.

The root of עם is the ayin alone, whose basic sense is movement, as set out under the root עה. The added mem makes it movement at one time, that is, existence at one time (in German, being at the same time, simultaneity), since the sign of existence is movement, and movement is in time, time being its foundation. So עם falls on the existence of two things under one relation: they share in the movement of what befalls them, that is, in existence, this one's lot like that one's.

גר.sense: Dragging (גרירה): a thing drawn along from place to place, not rolled; of the living, one with no fixed home who moves from place to place, a גר, sojourner.

more.t: Of things without life, dragging is slow flowing: וכמים הנגרים (Shmuel II 14:14), "like water that runs off"; ויגר מזה (Tehillim 75:9), "and He poured out of this"; עיני נגרה (Eichah 3:49), "my eye runs". What moves slowly is נוזל, flowing; what comes down drop by drop is נוטף, dripping; and what comes down slowly, neither fast nor drop by drop, is said to יגר, run down. So פרץ נחל מעם גר (Iyov 28:4), "a torrent broke out from where it trickled": from a place where the water only ran gently, a rushing stream burst out.

With a mem added, a bone that holds marrow is גרם, named for the marrow and the fatty juice that runs into it; a bone with no marrow is עץ, wood, since it has dried out like wood, as he explains at the root עץ. יששכר חמר גרם (Bereishis 49:14), "Yissachar is a donkey of bone", is a donkey whose bones have marrow in them. The verb, ועצמתיהם יגרם (Bamidbar 24:8), "and their bones he will drain", is doing something to their bones so as to suck out the marrow in them; and ואת חרשיה תגרמי (Yechezkel 23:34), "and you will suck its shards dry", is sucking out the juice that has run into them. אל גרם המעלות (Melachim II 9:13), "onto the gerem of the steps": the gerem is, as it seems, a kind of gutter into which the water off the roof runs.
So too the berry: שלשה גרגרים בראש אמיר (Yeshayahu 17:6), "three berries at the top of the bough". Each single berry of a fruit, into which the juice runs, is a גרגר.

כאבני גר מנפצות (Yeshayahu 27:9), "like stones of gir, smashed", are stones dragged about over the face of the field with no one to gather them. The verb is והגרתי לגי אבניה (Michah 1:6), "and I will drag her stones down into the valley"; and from the same sense, והגרם על ידי חרב (Yirmiyahu 18:21), "and drag them off by the power of the sword", and וכסאו לארץ מגרתה (Tehillim 89:45), "and his throne You dragged down to the ground", where מגרתה is like הגרת, You dragged, the mem standing in place of a heh.

גרון, the throat, is from dragging: קרא בגרון (Yeshayahu 58:1), "call out with the throat", so named because food and drink are dragged down from there into the belly. The windpipe, called גרגרת, bears the name too, because it is joined to the גרון: וענקים לגרגרתך (Mishlei 1:9), "and necklaces for your neck", since the גרגרת shows more on the outside than the גרון, which is the gullet.
The food dragged to the throat is גרה, the cud: מעלה גרה (Vayikra 11:4), "brings up the cud".

A small coin is also גרה: עשרים גרה השקל (Shemos 30:13), "the shekel is twenty gerah". It is named for dragging, because it is dragged constantly from hand to hand and never stays fixed in its place, unlike the heavy coins that are stored away in a treasury. The same is לאגורת כסף (Shmuel I 2:36), "for a piece of silver", a small coin of whatever kind.

אגרת, as את אגרת הפורים (Esther 9:29), "this letter of Purim", is a writing passed through the whole country from man to man to make its matter known in public. In parentheses he adds צירקולער, a circular.

The saw is מגרה, as מגררות במגרה (Melachim I 7:9), "sawn with a saw", named for the way it is used: not lifted like other tools but dragged over the wood, which splits apart. After this tool the language of the Talmud calls the חרש, the craftsman, נגר: נגר ולא בר נגר (Avodah Zarah 50b), "a carpenter and not a carpenter's son", the craftsman who works with the saw. A craftsman is always called after the tool he does most of his work with: the tailor is חייט after the חוט, the thread he sews with, and the shoemaker רצען after the מרצע, the awl; so the חרש is נגר because most of his work is with the saw.

Also from גרר is the verb אגר, gathering: a gathering that comes by dragging, collecting different things from different places, a little at a time. אגרה בקציר מאכלה (Mishlei 6:8), "she gathers her food in the harvest"; אגר בקיץ (Mishlei 10:5), "he gathers in summer"; ויין לא תשתה ולא תאגר (Devarim 28:39), "and wine you shall neither drink nor gather". The noun is מגרה: נהרסו ממגרות (Yoel 1:17), "the granaries are torn down", and העוד הזרע במגורה (Chaggai 2:19), "is the seed still in the granary?", a store gathered by dragging. Sometimes the alef drops: יגרהו בחרמו (Chavakuk 1:15), "he gathers him in his net", that is, יאגרהו ויאספנו, he gathers and collects him; יגורו עלי עזים (Tehillim 59:4), "the mighty gather against me", gathered against me from every side; and על דגן ותירוש יתגוררו (Hoshea 7:14), "over grain and wine they gather". The noun from it is מגור, as מגור מסביב (Tehillim 31:14), "dread on every side", formed like מקום, place, and מרום, height.

With a nun added, גרן, the threshing floor: גרן ויקב (Hoshea 9:2), "threshing floor and winepress"; כתבואת גרן (Bamidbar 18:30), "as the produce of the threshing floor". It is the place where grain not yet threshed is gathered. That is how it differs from the מגורה: the מגורה is the store of threshed grain, the גרן the store of unthreshed grain and of the sheaves.

From גר in its sense of gathering, the verb גור was borrowed for fear and dread: ויגר מואב (Bamidbar 22:3), "and Moav was in dread"; לא תגורו מפני איש (Devarim 1:17), "do not fear any man". Either it is gathering in to oneself, for fear of being exposed and spreading outward; or it is the gathering and collecting of all one's thoughts so as not to come to harm, as with יראה and מורא, fear, which, as he will explain in their place, come from seeing and watching.

מורא applies when the one afraid knows the one way he could be harmed and need only watch that way alone. מגור applies when the ways of harm are many, and he must gather all his thoughts and consider every way harm could possibly reach him. How the words of fear, מורא, מגור, חיל, אימתה ופחד (fear, dread, trembling, terror and fright), differ from each other is left to their own places.

Also from dragging is the verb גרה, provoking and quarrel: אל תתגרו בם (Devarim 2:5), "do not provoke them"; ואל תתגר בם מלחמה (Devarim 2:9), "and do not provoke them to war"; מתגרת ידך (Tehillim 39:11), "by the strife of Your hand"; איש חמה יגרה מדון (Mishlei 15:18), "a hot-tempered man stirs up strife", an act that drags quarrel and strife after it. It is close to חרחור, as אל תתחר במרעים (Tehillim 37:1), "do not grow heated over evildoers". But חרחור is from חרון, burning anger: the intent to do something that brings on burning wrath. גירוי, provoking, is the intent to do things that will draw one's fellow into dispute, and so it is a cause that drags the quarrel after it as its result. In the language of the Talmud a cause is גורם: זה וזה גורם (Pesachim 26b), "this and that both cause it"; דבר הגורם לממון (Pesachim 5b), "a thing that brings about money".

Of the living, dragging gives the noun גר: כי גר יהיה זרעך (Bereishis 15:13), "your seed will be strangers"; גר ותושב (Bereishis 23:4), "a stranger and a settler"; האזרח והגר (Vayikra 16:29), "the native and the stranger". גר describes one who sojourns in a land not his own, the opposite of the אזרח, who was born in the land where he is. A תושב is one not born here who has taken up his dwelling like one of the land's native-born; a גר is one not born here who also has no fixed home to settle in for all the days of his life.

אזרח is from זריחה, rising. The verb זרח marks the first appearing of anything, as והצרעת זרחה במצחו (Divrei HaYamim II 26:19), "and the tzaraas broke out on his forehead"; so the sun's first appearing on the horizon is called מזרח, as מזרח השמש (Yehoshua 1:15), "the rising of the sun". זריחה is not said once the sun already shines on the land, only of its first coming out and appearing on the horizon. So one who lives in the land of his birth is called אזרח, one found in the place where he rose and first appeared in the world. ומתערה כאזרח רענן (Tehillim 37:35), "spreading out like a fresh native", means like the rising, the first appearing, of a fresh tree, which right from the start of its growth is thick and stout and full of branches; there אזרח is a word that describes, not a noun.

more.h: גור, to sojourn and to dwell
more.t: The verb from גר: ויגר אברהם (Bereishis 21:34), "and Avraham sojourned"; האחד בא לגור (Bereishis 19:9), "this one came to sojourn"; לגור בארץ באנו (Bereishis 47:4), "we have come to sojourn in the land"; ארץ מגריהם (Shemos 6:4), "the land of their sojournings". It means dwelling that is not fixed. Sometimes it is said of fixed dwelling as well: אגורה באהלך עולמים (Tehillim 61:5), "I will dwell in Your tent forever"; לא יוסיפו לגור (Eichah 4:15), "they will dwell there no more".

From dwelling, the young of wild beasts is גור: גור אריה יהודה (Bereishis 49:9), "Yehudah is a lion's cub"; רבתה גוריה (Yechezkel 19:2), "she reared her cubs"; היניקו גוריהן (Eichah 4:3), "they suckled their young". It is called גור because it dwells in its den and its hole and does not yet go out to roam the land for prey, the grown beasts bringing it food. So ותעל אחד מגריה כפיר היה וילמד לטרף טרף (Yechezkel 19:3), "she brought up one of her cubs, he became a young lion and learned to tear prey": she brought one of her cubs up out of the hole, and it grew and became a כפיר, the lion that roams the villages, the כפרים, for food, and only afterwards learned to prey. Since the young lion preys more fiercely than the old, the tribes are likened, where preying is meant, to a lion's cub, a young lion, even though as long as it is a cub it does not prey.
